content: Dental caries, commonly known as tooth decay, is one of the most prevalent diseases affecting humans. It is estimated that up to 80% of individuals in high-income countries experience this condition. Caries progressively damages and destroys the tooth's tissues, including the dental pulp (nerve), leading to weakened teeth, aesthetic concerns, and impaired functionality. When caries progresses into the dentine and forms a cavity, treatment typically involves the placement of dental restorations, commonly referred to as fillings. This review serves as an update to a previous version published in 2009. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of adhesive bonding on the performance and longevity of dental amalgam restorations during their functional use. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Oral Health Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to January 21, 2016. Additionally, ongoing trials were identified through the US National Institutes of Health Trials Registry and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. No restrictions were applied regarding language or publication date during the search. The review focused on randomized controlled trials that compared adhesively bonded amalgam restorations to traditional non-bonded amalgam restorations. These trials were limited to adults with permanent molar and premolar teeth suitable for Class I and II amalgam restorations, using conventional cavity preparations designed for retention. Two independent reviewers screened the studies, extracted relevant data, and assessed the risk of bias in the included trial. Ultimately, only one trial met the inclusion criteria. This trial involved 31 patients who received a total of 113 restorations. At the two-year follow-up, 50 out of 53 restorations in the non-bonded group remained intact, while 55 out of 60 restorations in the bonded group survived, with five restorations unaccounted for. There was no statistically significant difference in post-insertion sensitivity between the two groups, either at baseline or at the two-year follow-up (P > 0.05). Additionally, no fractures of tooth tissue were reported, and there was no significant difference in marginal adaptation between the bonded and non-bonded restorations (P > 0.05). The authors concluded that there is no evidence to support or refute a difference in survival rates between bonded and non-bonded amalgam restorations. The single included trial, which was under-reported, did not demonstrate any significant differences in the performance of moderately sized adhesively bonded amalgam restorations compared to non-bonded restorations over a two-year period. Given the lack of evidence supporting additional benefits of adhesive bonding for amalgam restorations, clinicians should carefully consider the potential additional costs associated with this technique.
